title: Nine in 10 Indian Adults Have Abnormal Cholesterol Levels, Landmark ICMR Study Finds
excerpt: The largest-ever nationwide study on dyslipidemia reveals a public health crisis affecting nearly 90 percent of adults, with urban populations and northern states worst hit.
body:
• A new ICMR-INDIAB study covering 1.14 lakh adults across 31 states found that 89.8 percent of Indian adults have at least one form of dyslipidemia.
  • High LDL cholesterol — the 'bad' cholesterol linked to heart attacks — affects 67 percent of the population, with urban areas showing higher rates.
  • Northern Indian states including Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi recorded the worst numbers, while southern states fared slightly better.
  • The findings have implications for the global Indian diaspora, where cardiovascular disease is already the leading cause of death among South Asians.

A National Health Emergency

Nearly nine in every 10 Indian adults have abnormal cholesterol levels, according to the largest-ever nationwide study on lipid disorders published by the Indian Council of Medical Research. The ICMR-INDIAB study, which surveyed more than 1.14 lakh adults aged 20 and above across all 31 states and union territories, found that 89.8 percent of the population has at least one form of dyslipidemia — abnormal levels of fats in the blood that dramatically increase the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

The study, published in a leading medical journal, found that high LDL cholesterol — commonly called 'bad' cholesterol — affects 67 percent of Indian adults. Low HDL cholesterol, the protective 'good' cholesterol, was found in 45.3 percent of those studied, while elevated triglycerides affected 38.6 percent.

"The sheer scale of undiagnosed and untreated dyslipidemia in India constitutes a ticking time bomb for cardiovascular disease."

— ICMR-INDIAB Research Team

"Northern states including Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and Rajasthan recorded the highest prevalence of elevated LDL cholesterol, with rates exceeding 75 percent."

Geography of Risk

The study revealed stark regional disparities. Northern states including Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and Rajasthan recorded the highest prevalence of elevated LDL cholesterol, with rates exceeding 75 percent. Southern states such as Tamil Nadu and Kerala showed slightly lower but still alarming rates above 60 percent. Urban populations consistently outpaced rural ones across every category of lipid abnormality.

The findings also highlighted a gender gap. Men were more likely to have elevated triglycerides, while women showed higher rates of low HDL cholesterol, particularly after menopause. Age compounded the risk: prevalence rose steeply after 40, with those over 60 showing the highest rates of combined dyslipidemia.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Cardiovascular disease is the leading killer of South Asians worldwide, and the genetic predisposition that elevates risk among Indians does not disappear with emigration. Studies have consistently shown that Indian Americans, British Indians, and NRIs across the Gulf suffer heart attacks at younger ages and at lower body weights than other ethnic groups.

The ICMR findings underscore that the problem begins at home. Indians emigrating with undiagnosed cholesterol disorders carry elevated risk into their new countries, where dietary shifts toward processed foods and sedentary lifestyles can accelerate damage. Cardiologists have long recommended that South Asians begin lipid screening by age 20, earlier than standard Western guidelines suggest.

Dietary and Lifestyle Factors

Researchers pointed to several drivers: increased consumption of refined carbohydrates and cooking oils, declining physical activity in urban India, and a cultural resistance to routine blood testing. The traditional Indian diet, once protective with its emphasis on whole grains, lentils, and vegetables, has shifted sharply toward processed foods and excessive ghee and oil consumption in many households.

The study recommended population-level interventions including mandatory nutrition labeling, restrictions on trans fats in packaged foods, and public health campaigns promoting regular lipid testing — measures that India has been slow to implement compared to Western nations.

What's Next

The ICMR has recommended that India's national health program integrate routine lipid screening into primary healthcare, similar to existing programs for diabetes and hypertension. With cardiovascular disease already accounting for 28 percent of all deaths in India — roughly 6.3 million annually — the stakes could not be higher.

For NRIs, the takeaway is direct: get tested, know your numbers, and recognize that genetic risk does not stop at the border.
